newsitem.title: USA: National Semiconductor to acquire Cyrix.
newsitem.headline: National Semiconductor to acquire Cyrix.

text.p: National Semiconductor Corp. said Monday it agreed to buy Cyrix Corp. in a stock deal valued at $550 million, in a move that puts National on the map as an Intel competitor.

The move by National is also a big bet by the stodgy semiconductor company on the future of super-cheap personal computers and so-called information appliances. The Santa Clara, Calif.-based National is mostly known for its older, analogue components, and more recently for networking chips.
The companies said that they plan to develop new computer chip technology aimed at the low-cost personal computer - the sub-$500 market - and the information-appliance markets.

"We have now put into place all of the pieces and building blocks necessary to put a complete PC system on a chip ... Now it is truly possible to enable computing and the information age to reach the masses," said National Semi chief executive Brian Halla, on a conference call with reporters.
The companies said that their merger will allow them to offer chips for sub-$500 personal computers and that these low-cost devices could be on the market by early 1998.
A system-on-a-chip refers to a single processor that combines separate functions such as the core processor, memory, and logic functions, all on one chip.

"This changes the face of the company," said Drew Peck, a Cowen & Co. analyst. "The most interesting part of this deal is that National believes that the inevitable march of the PC is to the sub-$500 PC."
But in the interim, analysts said the deal will also be a huge boon to Cyrix, which has not been able to make big inroads as a developer of Intel Corp. clone microprocessors.

"Cyrix has lacked manufacturing," said Nathan Brookwood, a Dataquest Inc. analyst, adding that Cyrix is known as a "fab-less" semiconductor company, which has third parties do its manufacuturing. "National Semi can manufacture the parts that Cyrix has designed, that's a good thing for both."

Cyrix has also been under even more pressure in recent months, as Intel has been dropping prices sharply on its microprocessors, which dominate the PC market. And on Monday, Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Intel's biggest rival in the clone business, cut prices on its K6 Pentium-compatible chips.

"It's a good deal for Cyrix because they were going to fail if they didn't do something," said Peck of Cowen. "The price wars in the microprocessor business have gotten so bad they were going to fail if they didn't get their own manufacturing. ... National can do a better job selling the mainstream processors designed by Cyrix because they are considered a more reliable source."

Cyrix shareholders would receive 0.825 of a National Semiconductor share for each Cyrix share held. National Semiconductor stock closed down 6.25 cents at $33.4375 in New York Stock Exchange trading, while Cyrix closed up $1.8125 to $23.0625 in Nasdaq trading, and was up another $2 in after-hours trading.

The tax-free transaction, which still must be approved by Cyrix shareholders, is expected to be completed in November 1997. National said it would take an unspecified, one-time charge in that quarter.

National expects its acquisition of Cyrix to dilute its earnings per share in the third and fourth quarters of its current fiscal year, but said it will be accretive starting in the summer of next year.

Chief Financial Officer Donald Macleod said National would issue an additional 16 million shares as the merger is completed and those additional shares -- which will boost the full share count of the combined company by about 10 percent -- would effectively dilute earnings per share at first.

The deal is another example of consolidation in the chip industry. Earlier Monday, Intel, National Semiconductor's Santa Clara, Calif., rival, said it would buy Chips & Technologies Inc. for $420 million in cash.

Analysts said there will likely be even more consolidation in the industry, as more semiconductor firms seek to develop "system-on-a-chip" processors and bigger firms buy smaller firms with the technology to complete the missing pieces.

"A year from now, we could see a dramatic impact on the industry with these products," said Peck. "It has created quite a conundrum for the existing PC component manufacturers. It will be interesting to see how other manufacturers, including Intel, respond to the challenge."
